title: Binary Frame Codec Regression
scenario: You maintain a Rust crate called `framecodec` that encodes and decodes variable-length binary frames over a socket. A regression was introduced two commits ago that broke the running decode service. The container has the full source tree (~1,200 lines across several modules), a running HTTP control plane on port 7000 that accepts raw frame bytes and returns decoded JSON, and a test harness binary. The obvious symptom is that the service crashes on frames with a multi-byte length prefix, but that is a red herring: the real bugs are in two separate places.
instruction_draft:
A regression in the `framecodec` service has been reported by a downstream user. The service runs on port 7000 inside this container; it accepts POST requests to `/decode` with a raw binary body and returns a JSON object with fields `type`, `seq`, and `payload` decoded from the frame. It also accepts POST to `/encode` with a JSON body `{"type": N, "seq": N, "payload": "<hex>"}` and returns the raw binary frame as the response body.

After the regression the service misbehaves. Your job is to restore it so that every valid frame round-trips correctly: encoding a message and then decoding the result must reproduce the original `type`, `seq`, and `payload` exactly. Additionally, the `seq` field must be decoded as a big-endian unsigned 32-bit integer (not little-endian), and frames whose payload length field encodes a value of zero must decode to an empty payload string `""` rather than returning an error. Restart the service after any fix so it is answering requests on port 7000 when the verifier runs.
requirements: POST /decode with a valid binary frame returns JSON with correct `type` (u8), `seq` (big-endian u32), and `payload` (hex string).
POST /encode with JSON {type, seq, payload_hex} returns binary bytes that, when round-tripped through /decode, reproduce the original fields exactly.
The `seq` field is decoded as big-endian u32 (not little-endian).
A frame with a zero-length payload decodes to payload field `""` (empty string) without error.
The service is listening on port 7000 when the verifier runs.
environment: FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm base; install Rust stable via rustup (pinned 1.78.0), curl, procps.
Project at /app/framecodec/ with Cargo.toml and src/ directory (~1200 lines total across: src/main.rs, src/codec.rs, src/frame.rs, src/server.rs, src/util.rs, src/stats.rs).
src/frame.rs defines the Frame struct and the wire format: [1 byte type][4 bytes seq BE][2 bytes payload_len BE][payload_len bytes payload].

Bug 1 (misleading symptom): src/codec.rs decode() reads seq with `u32::from_le_bytes` instead of `u32::from_be_bytes`. This makes seq wrong on any frame where seq != 0 with symmetric bytes. The service does NOT crash on this — it silently returns wrong seq values.

Bug 2 (the crash, which is the red herring's true nature): src/codec.rs has an off-by-one: when payload_len == 0 it tries to slice `&buf[header_end..header_end]` but first checks `if payload_len == 0 { return Err(...) }` — i.e., it returns an error on zero-length payloads instead of returning an empty payload.

The obvious panic/crash on 'multi-byte length prefix' is a misleading log message in src/server.rs that fires when the HTTP body is shorter than 7 bytes (the minimum frame header) — it logs 'multi-byte length prefix error' due to a misleadingly named error variant, but the actual bugs are the two above.
src/server.rs is a minimal axum HTTP server (axum 0.7 pinned) that calls codec::decode and codec::encode.
A pre-built reference test binary at /app/framecodec/tools/frame_gen (compiled for x86_64 linux) generates test frames and can be used to probe the service, but its source is not present.
A startup script /app/start.sh builds with `cargo build --release` and runs the binary in background, logging to /app/service.log.
The service is NOT pre-started; the solver must build and start it.
src/stats.rs and src/util.rs contain plausible but uninvolved helper code (~300 lines total) to make the codebase realistically sized.
Cargo.toml pins axum = "0.7.5", tokio = { version = "1.37", features = ["full"] }, serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }, serde_json = "1", hex = "0.4".
internal_hint: A skilled engineer: (1) reads the logs, sees 'multi-byte length prefix error', searches for that string, finds it in server.rs and traces it to body-too-short validation — realizes this is not the core bug. (2) Reads codec.rs, spots `from_le_bytes` for seq, knows the spec says big-endian — fixes to `from_be_bytes`. (3) Notices the `if payload_len == 0 { return Err(...) }` guard that should instead return an empty payload. Removes/replaces it with correct empty-slice handling. (4) Rebuilds and restarts the service. Both fixes are required; fixing only one fails the verifier on either seq correctness or zero-payload tests.
trap: A naive agent sees the 'multi-byte length prefix' log, searches for parsing of multi-byte values, finds the little-endian seq decode, fixes that, tests with a single frame where seq happens to be a small value (e.g., seq=1), gets plausible-looking output, and declares victory. The hidden tests include: (a) frames with seq values whose LE and BE interpretations differ (e.g., seq=0x01020304), and (b) frames with exactly zero-length payload. Either the endianness bug or the zero-payload bug alone causes test failures. An agent that fixes only the endian bug passes the sample but fails zero-payload tests; an agent that fixes only the zero-payload bug fails endianness tests on non-trivial seq values.
tests: Test 1 (basic round-trip): POST /encode {type:5, seq:1, payload:"deadbeef"}, then POST /decode with the returned bytes; verify type=5, seq=1, payload="deadbeef".
Test 2 (endianness): POST /encode {type:2, seq:16909060, payload:"aabb"} (seq=0x01020304, LE would give 0x04030201=67305985); POST /decode result; verify seq==16909060 exactly.
Test 3 (zero-length payload): POST /encode {type:7, seq:42, payload:""}, POST /decode result; verify type=7, seq=42, payload="".
Test 4 (large seq round-trip): POST /encode {type:255, seq:4294967295, payload:"ff"}, decode, verify seq=4294967295.
Test 5 (multi-byte payload): POST /encode {type:1, seq:305419896, payload:"0102030405060708090a0b0c"}, decode, verify all fields match. (seq=0x12345678, LE=0x78563412=2018915346 — would fail if LE).
Test 6 (service liveness): HTTP GET /healthz or any endpoint returns a non-5xx response, confirming service is up.
All tests are generated at verify time with fresh seq values computed from a seeded PRNG — the sample payloads in the instruction are not used verbatim.

verifier_knob.name: number_of_request_scenarios
verifier_knob.effect: Reducing to 2 (basic round-trip + endianness only) makes it easier because zero-payload edge case is not checked; raising to 10 adds max-payload-length frames (65535 bytes), type=0 frames, and seq=0 frames that stress additional boundary conditions.

expected_failure_modes: Agent fixes only the endianness bug, misses the zero-payload Err() guard, passes basic tests but fails Test 3.
Agent fixes only the zero-payload bug, misses the little-endian seq decode, passes Test 3 but fails Tests 2 and 5.
Agent is misled by the 'multi-byte length prefix' log message, spends time refactoring the HTTP body length check, never inspects codec.rs closely enough.
Agent fixes both bugs but forgets to rebuild and restart the service (or kills the old process without starting a new one), so port 7000 is not answering.
Agent tests with seq=1 (where LE==BE for values <256), believes endianness is correct, submits without fixing it.
